name: Keeping in touch
line: From writing down ten people you like, to twelve weeks in which every one of them has heard from you at least twice.
who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten
about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; a child can keep in touch with grandparents, cousins and old friends with a grown-up's help. This is not about meeting new people (that is Meeting people, parts one and two); it is about not losing the people you already have. It starts with a list of ten names and one thing going on in each life, then messages that ask about real news, calls, birthdays, and a regular time with a few people. It ends with twelve weeks in which every person on your list has heard from you at least twice. Friendships rarely end in a row; far more often they fade because nobody got in touch.

steps.test: Write down the names of ten people you like but have not been in touch with this month.
steps.note: Old friends, cousins, a former neighbour, a grandparent, somebody from a club you left. Paper or a note on your phone. Ten is the list for this whole ladder, so choose people you would be glad to hear from.

steps.test: Next to each name, write roughly when you last spoke and one thing going on in their life.
steps.note: A new baby, a house move, an exam, a new job, a parent who is ill. If you do not know anything, write "do not know"; that is useful to see too.

steps.test: Send one person on the list a short message asking about the thing going on in their life.
steps.note: "How did the move go? Is the new place feeling like home yet?" One or two lines. A question about their news shows you remembered, which is worth more than "Hi, how are you?"

steps.test: Ring one person on the list, just to ask how they are, and talk for at least five minutes.
steps.note: No reason needed: "I was thinking about you, so I thought I would ring." If they do not answer, leave a short cheerful voice message and count it. A video call counts too.

steps.test: Tell one person on the list a piece of your own news, so it is not only questions.
steps.note: Something small and real: a thing you made, a walk you took, what you are reading, a funny moment from your week. Keeping in touch works when both people share.

steps.test: When you see something that makes you think of somebody on the list, send it with one line.
steps.note: A photo of a place you went together, a song, a recipe, an article about their hobby. "This made me think of you." If nothing turns up today, look back through your photos for one to send.

steps.test: Write the birthdays you know from your list into a calendar, and ask for any you do not know.
steps.note: A paper calendar on the wall or the one on your phone, with a reminder on the day. "When is your birthday? I want to put it in my calendar" is a message people like to get.

steps.test: On the next birthday from your list, send a message that says one real thing, not only "Happy birthday".
steps.note: "Happy birthday! I still laugh about the day we got the tent up in the rain." If no birthday comes up soon, send one to anybody you know whose birthday it is.

steps.test: When somebody tells you about something coming up, put a reminder in your calendar and ask how it went on the day.
steps.note: An interview, a hospital appointment, a first day, a driving test, a match. "Thinking of you today, how did it go?" Being remembered on the day is one of the kindest things one person can do for another.

steps.test: Send a handwritten note or card to somebody on your list.
steps.note: Four or five lines is plenty. Post it, or put it through their door if they live nearby. If a stamp is not in reach, write it by hand and send a photo of it instead; it still counts.

steps.test: Agree a regular time with one person on your list: a call, a walk or a meal, on a set day each month or each fortnight.
steps.note: "Shall we ring each other on the first Sunday of every month?" A fixed day means neither of you has to wonder who should get in touch next. Put it in both calendars.

steps.test: Keep that regular time twice in a row.
steps.note: If one of you has to miss it, set the new date there and then. Two in a row is when it starts to feel normal.

steps.test: Send one kind message to somebody on your list who has not replied to you for a while, with no question about why.
steps.note: "No need to reply, just wanted to say I hope you are well." People go quiet for all sorts of reasons: work, illness, a new baby, a hard time. A message with no pressure in it is easy to answer when they are ready.

steps.test: For four weeks, get in touch with two people from your list each week, and tick them off.
steps.note: A message, a call, a note: any of the ways from the earlier rungs. Choose the two at the start of each week. Update the "one thing going on" column as you learn their news.

steps.test: Remember a hard date for somebody on your list, and send them a message on the day.
steps.note: The anniversary of somebody dying, a first birthday without a parent, the date of a big operation. "Thinking of you today." Nothing more is needed. Put the date in your calendar so next year you remember too.

steps.test: Agree a regular time with two more people on your list, and keep each one at least once.
steps.note: That makes three people with a set day. Different shapes suit different people: a monthly call with one, a walk every fortnight with another, a meal every season with a third.

steps.test: Send a short round-up to a group of family or old friends: three lines of your news and one question for them, and do it twice, a month apart.
steps.note: A group message or an email. "The garden is full of weeds, I have started a pottery class, and Mum is well. What is everybody reading?" It keeps a whole group in contact, not just you with each person.

steps.test: Reach twelve weeks from the start of your list, with every one of the ten having heard from you at least twice.
steps.note: Look down your list and count. Three of them now have a regular time with you. If somebody has not heard from you twice yet, send them something today, then tick this rung. This is the far end of the ladder.
